title: Is Zorin OS the Right Linux Distro for Windows Refugees? A Deep Dive
excerpt: With 2 million downloads in 3 months, Zorin OS is leading the Windows-to-Linux migration. Here's what you need to know before making the switch.
content:
The Great Migration Has Begun

Something remarkable is happening in the world of desktop computing. Since Microsoft ended mainstream support for Windows 10 on October 14, 2025, millions of users have been forced into an uncomfortable decision: upgrade to Windows 11 on hardware that may not support it, pay Microsoft for extended security updates, or try something entirely different. A surprising number are choosing door number three — and they're landing on Zorin OS.

Zorin OS 18, released strategically on the exact same day Windows 10 support ended, has surpassed 2 million downloads in under three months. According to the Zorin team, over 75% of those downloads originated from Windows machines. That's not a small blip on the radar — it's one of the largest Linux adoption events in desktop history.

Our co-founder Robert Braxman recently took a deep, hands-on look at Zorin OS to answer the question everyone's asking: is it actually good enough for people coming from Windows? The short answer is yes — but the full picture is more nuanced than that.

Why Windows Users Are Leaving — And Why It Matters

Let's be clear about what's driving this migration. Microsoft's Windows 11 hardware requirements — particularly the TPM 2.0 mandate and strict CPU compatibility lists — have locked out an estimated 240 million PCs from upgrading. These aren't broken machines. They're perfectly functional computers that Microsoft has effectively declared obsolete.

According to Tom's Hardware, those 240 million PCs could generate roughly 1.06 billion pounds of e-waste — enough to stack 372 miles higher than the moon. A Georgia Tech study noted that this is a textbook case of planned obsolescence, where companies design products with intentionally short lifespans to drive consumption.

But the hardware lockout is only half the story. Windows 11 has intensified data collection to levels that should concern anyone who values their digital autonomy. The operating system tracks application usage patterns, typing behavior, voice input, and how you interact with your device. Features like Recall, Copilot, and targeted advertising are baked into the system. Even at the lowest telemetry settings, Windows 11 sends "non-negotiable" diagnostic data to Microsoft's servers — and cybersecurity researchers have documented that the Diagnostic Data Viewer only shows a small fraction of the thousands of data points actually being collected.

For privacy-conscious users, sticking with Windows isn't just inconvenient — it's a compromise you make with every keystroke.

What Zorin OS Gets Right

Robert's review found that Zorin makes some genuinely smart design decisions that lower the barrier for Windows users. The desktop layout positions the taskbar at the bottom, puts a start-menu-style launcher where you'd expect it, and uses rounded corners and system tray icons that feel familiar. It's not a pixel-perfect Windows clone — and it doesn't pretend to be — but it's close enough that the initial shock of switching to Linux is significantly reduced.

But the real wins go beyond surface-level aesthetics:

  • App installation is dramatically better. When you click on a .deb file in Zorin, it actually launches an installer with full app information. On Ubuntu, clicking a .deb file opens it as a read-only archive — confusing for anyone who's never used Linux. Zorin also handles AppImage files properly, prompting for permissions directly instead of requiring terminal commands like apt install libfuse2 and manual permission changes.
  • Flatpak by default. This is perhaps the most meaningful technical decision Zorin makes. Instead of Ubuntu's proprietary Snap format, Zorin defaults to Flatpak — the open, community-driven package format. You still get the choice between Flatpak, Snap, and .deb when installing apps, but the default matters.
  • Fewer installation prompts. The Zorin installer is noticeably simpler than Ubuntu's, with fewer decisions to make and sensible defaults throughout. Robert noted that there's nothing in the installation process that would confuse a novice user.
  • Consistent with Ubuntu under the hood. Since Zorin is a close fork of Ubuntu, any troubleshooting guide or fix written for Ubuntu will work on Zorin. This is huge for new users who rely on search engines to solve problems.

Why the Flatpak Choice Matters for Your Privacy

Zorin's decision to default to Flatpak over Snap deserves special attention, because it's not just a technical preference — it's a privacy decision.

Snap packages are controlled through Canonical's centralized, proprietary Snap Store. Privacy Guides community members have documented that Snap packages include built-in telemetry, sending install and usage data back to Canonical. Beyond the telemetry, Snaps mount themselves as virtual volumes on your system, cluttering your storage device view. They also suffer from notably slower startup times — in one benchmark, Firefox via Snap took 11 seconds to launch compared to under one second via Flatpak.

Flatpak, by contrast, is fully open source with a decentralized repository model. It enforces sandboxing by default and doesn't include built-in telemetry. Anyone can host a Flatpak repository, which means no single company controls the ecosystem. For those of us who believe software distribution shouldn't be a surveillance opportunity, Flatpak is the clear winner.

Where Zorin Falls Short

Robert's review wasn't all praise. A few areas still need work:

  • Codec installation is confusing. Like Ubuntu, Zorin doesn't ship with all media codecs due to licensing restrictions. Zorin attempts to solve this with a codec section in their software app, but the options — labeled things like "GStreamer this-or-that" — are incomprehensible to most users. Robert's advice? Just run sudo apt install ubuntu-restricted-extras in the terminal and move on.
  • Updates lag behind Ubuntu. Zorin is a small team based in Ireland. Ubuntu is currently on 24.04, with 26.04 LTS arriving in April. Zorin 18 only just caught up to Ubuntu 24.04 — roughly 1.5 years behind. For most users, this delay doesn't matter since they still receive Ubuntu security updates. But if you're running brand-new hardware with bleeding-edge driver requirements, the delay could be an issue.
  • The USB installer hangs without explanation. During installation, Zorin verifies the USB media integrity before proceeding — a good security practice. But it doesn't communicate what it's doing, leaving users staring at an apparently frozen screen. A simple progress message would fix this.
  • Thunderbird isn't included by default. Unlike Ubuntu, Zorin doesn't pre-install the Thunderbird email client. For our community, where encrypted email communication is a priority, this means an extra installation step.

The Bigger Picture: Why This Migration Could Reshape Computing

The numbers tell a compelling story. Windows Central reports that desktop Linux in the United States crossed the 5% market share threshold in June 2025 according to StatCounter. Globally, Linux remains in the low single digits for desktop share, but the trend line is unmistakable — and Windows 10's end of life could be the inflection point.

But let's think about what's really at stake here. Every Windows user who migrates to Linux is a user who escapes Microsoft's ever-expanding data collection apparatus. They're moving from an operating system that monitors their typing patterns, pushes AI features that process their data, and buries opt-out settings in layers of menus — to an operating system where they have genuine control over what leaves their machine.

Could Microsoft make this worse in the future? Absolutely. The trajectory is clear: more AI integration, more cloud dependency, more data collection, fewer ways to opt out. Every Windows update seems to push further in this direction. Linux offers an exit from that trajectory entirely.

Of course, downloads don't equal permanent migrations. Two million downloads is impressive, but the real question is how many of those users stay on Linux. That depends on application compatibility, which has improved massively with Wine 10 (released in 2025 with better Vulkan, Direct3D, and Wayland support), and on the continued investment by communities like ours in making privacy-respecting technology accessible.

What You Can Do

If you're still running Windows 10 — or even Windows 11 — and you care about your privacy, here's our honest advice:

  • Try Zorin OS first if you're new to Linux. Based on Robert's review, we're now recommending Zorin over stock Ubuntu for users coming from Windows. The smoother installation process, better app handling, and Flatpak-first approach make it the better starting point.
  • Download Zorin Core (free) from zorin.com. If you want installation support, the Pro version at $47.99 includes direct help — worth it if you're not comfortable with the technical side.
  • Flash the ISO to a USB drive using Balena Etcher. Don't just copy the file — you need to flash it to create a bootable drive.
  • Boot from USB via Windows Recovery. On Windows 11: Start → Settings → System → Recovery → Advanced Startup → Restart. On Windows 10: Start → Settings → Update & Security → Recovery → Advanced Startup → Restart Now. Then select "Use a device" and choose your USB drive.
  • Choose "Erase disk" during installation for a clean break from Windows. If you want to keep Windows alongside Linux, watch Robert's dual boot guide from December 2025.
  • After installation, run sudo apt install ubuntu-restricted-extras to get all media codecs.
  • Opt out of Zorin's minimal telemetry during installation, or remove it later with sudo apt remove zorin-os-census.

The path from Windows to Linux has never been smoother. Zorin OS isn't perfect, but it's close enough to Ubuntu that you get the hardware compatibility and community support of the world's most popular desktop Linux, wrapped in an interface that won't leave you lost on day one.

Privacy isn't a feature you can bolt on to an operating system built for surveillance. It has to be the foundation. Linux gives you that foundation — and Zorin makes it accessible.
